questions.passage:
Elves

Elves have been a popular subject in fiction for centuries, ranging from W. Shakespeare's play "A Midsummer Night's Dream" to the classic fantasy novels of J. R. R. Tolkien 300 years later. But it's only recently that elves have been confined to plays, books, and fairy tales. In centuries past, belief in the existence of fairies and elves was common among both adults and children.

Like fairies, elves were said to be magical, tiny shape changers. Shakespeare's elves were tiny, winged creatures that lived in, and playfully flitted around flowers. English male elves were described as looking like little old men, though elf maidens were invariably young and beautiful. Like men of the time, elves lived in kingdoms found in forests, meadows, or hollowed-out tree trunks. [A]

Elves, fairies and leprechauns are closely related in folklore, though elves specifically seem to have sprung from early Norse mythology. By the 1500s, people began incorporating elf folklore into stories and legends about fairies, and by 1800, fairies and elves were widely considered to be simply different names for the same magical creatures. [B]

As with fairies, elves eventually developed a reputation for pranks and mischief, and strange daily occurrences were often attributed to them. For example, when the hair on a person or horse became tangled and knotted, such "elf locks" were blamed on elves. [C]

Though elves were sometimes friendly toward humans, they were also known to take terrible revenge on any human who offends them. They may steal babies, cattle, milk, and bread or enchant and hold young men in their spell for years at a time.

Another type of elf emerged, one with a somewhat different nature and form than the mischievous and tiny ones of old. Some elves, such as those depicted in J.R.R. Tolkien's "Lord of the Rings" trilogy, are slender, human-sized, and beautiful, with fine, almost angelic, features. Tolkien's characters were drawn largely from his research into Scandinavian folklore, and therefore it's not surprising that his elves might be tall and blond. Though not immortal, these elves were said to live hundreds of years. They have also become a staple of modern fantasy fiction. [D]

In either form, elves are strongly associated with magic and nature. As with fairies, elves were said to secretly steal healthy human babies and replace them with their own kind. There were even legends instructing parents on how to get their real child back from its elven abductors.

Each generation seems to have their own use for elves in their stories. Just as leprechauns have historically been associated with one type of work (shoemaking), it is perhaps not surprising that many common (and commercial) images of elves depict them as industrious workers; think, for example, of Santa Claus' toy making elves. Folklore, like language and culture, is constantly evolving, and elves will likely always be with us, in one form or another.

questions.explanation: "It is + period + since + past simple": the last time he won was four years ago.

questions.explanation: Present simple is used for timetables and scheduled departures: "My plane leaves at 10 am."

questions.explanation: "Not only … but … as well" — as well (= too) goes at the end of the clause.

questions.q: Those women, ______ are my students, work at the local hospital.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clause with possessive: "whose children are my students".

questions.q: While she ______ to convince him of her innocence, he flatly refused to listen.
questions.explanation: Past continuous after "while" for the action in progress when the past-simple action ("refused") happened.

questions.q: The accident which happened this morning ______ to the police.
questions.explanation: Passive: the accident cannot report itself — "was reported to the police".

questions.q: "Would you like some more tea?" "Yes please, but only ______."
questions.explanation: Tea is uncountable, and the speaker wants a small amount: "only a little".

questions.q: Do you know ______ Bob is coming to the show tomorrow?
questions.explanation: Reported yes/no question: "Do you know whether Bob is coming…?"

questions.q: ______, there has been no increase in bus fares since last year.
options: It is enough of a surprise
questions.explanation: A sentence adverb introduces a comment on the whole statement: "Surprisingly enough, there has been no increase…".

questions.q: A true friend is someone you can always trust and ______.
questions.explanation: "Trust and rely on" — rely on someone means depend on them.

questions.q: Unless ______ increases, the factory will close down.
questions.explanation: A factory survives if its production (output) increases.

questions.q: Hugo has been in a bad ______ since he broke up with Mary.
questions.explanation: "In a bad mood" is the fixed expression for feeling unhappy or irritable.

questions.q: It's time something was done for the millions of children who are ______ to death.
questions.explanation: "Starving to death" is the collocation — dying from lack of food.

questions.q: I wish I could go abroad, but my passport has ______.
questions.explanation: A passport expires when it is no longer valid; "stolen" would need the passive (has been stolen).

questions.q: Dave survived the accident, but his car was ______.
questions.explanation: Things are damaged; people are injured.

questions.q: That green jacket is ______ what I've been looking for. How much is it?
questions.explanation: "Exactly what I've been looking for" — exactly emphasises a precise match.

questions.q: Daniel is very depressed as he has been ______ since the factory closed.
questions.explanation: "Out of work" means unemployed — he lost his job when the factory closed.

questions.q: The police didn't arrest him because they had no ______ that he was involved in the crime.
questions.explanation: "Have no proof that…" — evidence showing he was involved.

questions.q: You must have ______ in your abilities if you want to do this job well.
questions.explanation: "Have confidence in your abilities" — confidence in is the collocation.

questions.explanation: "Have no intention of + V-ing" = not plan to do something.

questions.q:
Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given (no more than FIVE words).
You ought to tell Martin what happened. (BETTER)
→ You ______ Martin know what happened.
questions.explanation: "Ought to" ≈ "had better" (advice), and "let somebody know" = tell somebody.

questions.q:

Paul finds it difficult to look for a suitable job. (HAS)
→ Paul ______ for a suitable job.
questions.explanation: "Find it difficult to do" = "have difficulty (in) doing".

questions.q:

The kids continued to play tennis despite the fact that it was raining. (CARRIED)
→ The kids ______ despite the fact that it was raining.
questions.explanation: "Carry on + V-ing" = continue doing.

questions.q:
Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given (no more than FIVE words).
Although Henry thought of the plan, he didn't get the credit for it. (CAME)
→ Even ______ the plan, he didn't get the credit for it.
questions.explanation: "Even though" = although, and "come up with" = think of (an idea/plan).

questions.q:
Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given (no more than FIVE words).
It was such a high shelf that the little girl couldn't reach it. (LOW)
→ The shelf ______ for the little girl to reach.
questions.explanation: "Such a high shelf that she couldn't reach" → "not low enough for her to reach" (adjective + enough + for + to-infinitive).

questions.q:

They will work this weekend, but only if you pay them extra. (UNLESS)
→ This weekend, they ______ are paid extra.
questions.explanation: "Only if you pay them" → "unless they are paid": unless = if … not.

questions.q:
Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given (no more than FIVE words).
You can use margarine instead of butter in this recipe. (USED)
→ Margarine ______ place of butter in this recipe.
questions.explanation: Passive with modal: "can be used", and "in place of" = instead of.

questions.q:

People say he is the richest man in the region. (SAID)
→ He ______ richest man in the region.
questions.explanation: Personal passive of reporting verbs: "People say he is…" → "He is said to be…".

questions.q:
